problem.title: Large-scale document classification
problem.context: An insurer classifies 2–8 million documents daily into 60 claim types using an approved-provider LLM. Demand rises fourfold during storm season. Claims handling, fraud investigation and analytics consume results; documents contain personal data.

requirements.text: Classify every incoming document into a claim type, with a confidence.
Deliver the results to the three consuming teams.
Send the documents the classifier is unsure about to human review, and use the reviewers' corrections to improve the classifier.
During storm season, at eight million documents a day, every document is classified within two hours of arrival.
When classification quality drops for one claim type (for example, after a form changes its layout), operators see it within one day.
The classification costs less than 0.2 cents per document on average over the year.
A consuming team can change how it processes the results without the other teams or the classifier having to change.
The documents contain personal data and may not leave the EU.
The classifier uses an LLM from the insurer's approved provider, in its EU region.

points.description: Scheduled jobs consume privacy- and policy-validated data arriving through messaging channels, scale compute elastically, score models in batches, and persist results for storage or analytics. A REST prediction microservice exposes model outputs, while monitoring tracks feature-generation changes, schemas, statistics, and unusual inputs to inform corrective action. Trade-off: This gains operational scalability, governed data handling, and visibility into input drift, but batch scoring may reduce freshness and responsiveness compared with fully online prediction. Supporting REST access alongside scheduled deployment may also add interface and operational complexity.

Streaming feature ingestion feeds privacy- and policy-validated data into an elastic, containerized prediction cluster fronted by a queue. A REST microservice exposes predictions, while continuous quality monitoring observes served behavior as demand changes. Trade-off: This provides scalable throughput, low-latency access, governed data handling, and rapid quality visibility, but adds operational complexity across queues, containers, streaming pipelines, autoscaling, and monitoring. It also depends on timely labels for quality measurement and may cost more than simpler batch or static serving.

Solution: Policy-validated data arrives through messaging channels and feeds a REST prediction microservice implemented as serverless functions. The runtime scales to zero when idle, while deployed predictions receive human oversight for review and intervention. Trade-off: Serverless scale-to-zero reduces idle cost and capacity management, but can introduce startup latency and less predictable performance. Privacy checks and human review improve governance and accountability, but add processing overhead and operational effort.

Scheduled jobs consume privacy- and policy-validated records from messaging channels, scale compute elastically as workload changes, and write predictions to storage or analytics systems. A REST prediction microservice can expose model outputs, while human reviewers oversee production behavior and intervene when needed. Trade-off: This combines scalable, governed, reviewable operations with durable batch results and API access, but scheduled scoring sacrifices immediate freshness and elastic scaling can increase infrastructure cost; human oversight also adds operational effort and potential review delays.

A REST prediction microservice runs containerized predictors behind a queue, while elastic resources scale the serving cluster as streaming feature demand changes. Privacy- and policy-validated ingestion feeds predictions, with human reviewers overseeing production behavior and interventions. Trade-off: This combines responsive, scalable serving with governed data handling and operational accountability, but adds queueing, orchestration, compliance-validation, and human-review overhead. Human oversight may also limit fully automated response speed and increase operating cost.

A serverless REST prediction service receives continuously ingested features, scales execution with demand, and uses policy-validated data and pipelines. Human reviewers oversee deployed predictions and intervene when needed. Trade-off: This combines elastic capacity, low idle cost, and stronger privacy and policy control, but scale-to-zero can introduce cold-start latency and less predictable responsiveness for streaming workloads. Human oversight improves control but adds review effort and can limit throughput.

adrs.title: Prediction serving and delivery
adrs.context: The workload needs high-volume classification and delivery to three teams. The space provides serving patterns and a REST boundary, but does not define confidence output or independent consumer subscriptions.

options.name: Scheduled batch
pros: Scales scheduled scoring and persists results for downstream use.
cons: Freshness depends on schedule; exact two-hour completion is unproven.

options.name: Queue-fronted online
pros: Queueing and distributed predictors support low-latency throughput.
cons: Adds operational components and has no measured storm throughput.

options.name: Serverless deployment
pros: Managed execution adapts to variable demand.
cons: Cold-start and concurrency behavior are unmeasured.

options.name: REST interface
cons: Does not itself establish loose coupling among consumers.
options.reason: All three alternatives expose a service boundary.

adrs.title: Capacity and seasonal cost
adrs.context: Storm season multiplies volume, while average cost has a strict ceiling. No available value proves either numeric target; capacity strategy must be validated against representative load and annual cost.

options.name: Elastic scaling
cons: May raise costs under sustained peak load.
options.reason: A1 and B1 select elastic capacity for seasonal changes.

options.name: Scale to zero
cons: Can add startup delay and does not bound peak cost.

adrs.title: Monitoring and uncertain cases
adrs.context: The system must route uncertain classifications for review and use the corrections to improve the classifier. Human oversight is a partial match; it does not specify confidence thresholds, correction capture, or retraining. The competing drift-monitoring option can surface input changes but does not implement the review workflow.

options.name: Input drift monitoring
pros: Can surface schema and input distribution changes.
cons: Does not route uncertain predictions or verify classification quality by claim type.
options.reason: P1 exposes the monitoring-first batch hypothesis.

options.name: Real-time quality monitoring
pros: Measures quality behavior when labels are available.
cons: Needs timely labels and does not define human correction feedback.

options.name: Human oversight
pros: Provides a human intervention path for predictions.
cons: Does not alone implement threshold routing or retraining from corrections.
options.reason: All final alternatives prioritize human review.

adrs.title: Personal data governance and ingestion
adrs.context: Personal data requires policy controls and the workload needs an ingestion path suited to batch or streaming. The space contains a privacy-validation value but cannot guarantee EU residency.

options.name: Messaging plus policy validation
pros: Supports queued data delivery and policy checks.
options.reason: Batch and serverless seeds use messaging input with validation.

options.name: Streaming plus policy validation
pros: Supports continuous input for responsive serving.
cons: Does not guarantee EU-only processing or end-to-end latency.
options.reason: B1 uses streaming ingestion with validation.

unaddressed.note: The design space has no decision about selecting the insurer-approved LLM provider or enforcing its EU region.

The selected points use human oversight to support the explicit uncertain-case review workflow. They do not select input or prediction-quality monitoring, so a claim-type quality drop within one day is not established.
